Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are dominated by black holes, and the characteristics of their mass and spin can be ascertained through the analysis of specific emission lines in their electromagnetic spectra, particularly those arising from the broad full-width half-max (FWHM) of the emission lines, which provide constraints on the velocities and velocities' orientations of the emitting material. However, the interpretation of these spectra is complicated by the diverse and intricate nature of the emission regions around AGNs. Utilizing a radiative transfer code, we have developed and examined spectral models that correspond to various geometries and physical conditions, and we have explored the impact of different full (FWHM) definitions on the estimation of line widths, and their implications for the estimation of the mass and spin of the central black hole. Utilizing the full FWHM of the broad H$\beta$ line, we have found that the emission from AGNs can be used to estimate the mass and spin of the central black hole, within the context of simplified spherical models. Furthermore, we have found that the full (FWHM) of other spectral lines, such as [O III], Mg II, and Fe XXV, can be used to estimate the mass and spin of the central black hole, within the context of more complex models. Furthermore, we have found that the estimation of the full (FWHM) of these lines is influenced by the structure and physical conditions of the emitting regions, which can introduce systematic biases in the derived

A distinctive feature of neural development is the oscillation of cell nuclei between the inner and outer layers of the neuroepithelium as part of interkinetic nuclear migration. While the occurrence of this phenomenon is well-documented, a complete understanding of the underlying mechanisms remains elusive. Here, we present several approaches to precisely quantify the migration pattern, incorporating features like average position, speed, and the distances traveled both vertically and horizontally. Furthermore, we demonstrate how continuous and discrete models can be employed to analyze the data, providing estimates for the time spent in different locations, varying based on position, depth, and location. Moreover, we suggest that a continuous model can be used to generate a mathematical data that reflects the relationship between position and time, which can then be incorporated into generalized linear models to investigate possible explanatory factors.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured, and contain non-zero diagonal elements, result in performance limitations in current reconstruction algorithms due to their complex relationships. To overcome this, this research proposes a novel method, Code Structure Unfolding, which leverages the inherent properties of code patterns to decouple their structured patterns from images, thereby enabling the use of highly efficient, diagonal code patterns for subsequent high-performance image reconstruction. Furthermore, images and non-diagonal code structure can be independently reconstructed through efficient optimization, leading to superior performance in recovered image quality. Extensive experiments on video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing demonstrate that Code Unfolding achieves comparable or even better reconstruction results compared to state-of-the-art methods using non-diagonal patterns, while also offering computational efficiency gains of orders of magnitude.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

The growth of information technology has led to an increased reliance on personal data, which is now frequently presented in ID card form. To facilitate the digitization of this information, a novel approach employing deep learning is proposed for extracting text from ID cards. Initially, an open-source toolbox for ID card text recognition is developed, which utilizes a state-of-the-art system for optical character recognition. Subsequently, a high-quality ID card text extraction framework is proposed, taking advantage of the ID card's consistent layout. This framework comprises three key components: a novel machine translation model for Id2Text based on a custom dataset, an Id2Text quality assessment model, and Id2Text quality refinement based on machine scoring.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. The lattice discretization method showed high accuracy in reconstructing the harmonic oscillator's ground state wavefunction and comparing simulated and analytical momentum distributions. The time-dependent case saw similar results, with the lambda phi coupling method successfully capturing the oscillator's response to time-varying drives.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, we collected precise photometric data from four different observatories for the asteroid 2867 Šteins for nearly a year, obtaining over 4000 light curves and corresponding rotational information from multiple epochs. The resulting data allowed us to estimate the period change rate and its uncertainty, revealing strong evidence for the Yarkovsky-O'keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect on this particular asteroid. Furthermore, thermal models were developed to explain the thermal inertia of the surface and possible surface properties, such as the Yarkovsky effect's reliance on surface asymmetry. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the Yarkovsky effect, the thermal behavior of the surface, and the long-term orbital evolution of this binary near-Earth asteroid.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically isomorphic to a compact group. Furthermore, when the surface's boundary is not empty, the subgroup of homeomorphisms that do move the boundary surface and have compact boundary behavior is not even topologically isomorphic to a compact topological group in the compact-open topological space, while for a closed surface of a higher genus than a torus, the boundary-fixing homeomorphisms' topological space is maximally non-Iso.

A regularity theory for the effective topological space $\Sigma_r^0$ has been proposed to be analogous to Fox's computable topology. A key feature of this theory is that there is a direct correlation between being computable and being continuous for functions that are classified as regular. Furthermore, the relationship between being regular and being computable for more complex topological spaces can be established using the fact that topological closure and union operations are both computable within it.

A machine learning technique called reservoir computing generates a model that can efficiently process data and process complex operations, leaving only a reduced set of adjustable parameters for optimization. Presley Taylor's fourth-generation variation of this approach, called g4rc, entirely utilizes a different, harder-to-squeeze relationship between input and output for its prediction, with potential improvements over earlier versions in required training data, prediction accuracy, and handling noisy inputs. Using G4RC, required training data for various tasks has been reduced while maintaining high levels of accuracy, including a significant improvement of 2 orders of magnitude, in contrast to earlier methods. Moreover, G4RC demonstrates superior handling of noisy inputs, resulting in more accurate outputs even when they contain up to 50% noise.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain unclear, with recent neuroimaging studies showing consistent patterns of continuous animacy representation.  Two main hypotheses attempt to explain this phenomenon: the distinctiveness hypothesis posits that objects with unique structural features stand out, whereas the complexity hypothesis suggests that objects with numerous parts require more processing due to interconnected relationships.  Using functional and structural MRI data from sixteen human participants, we found support for the complexity hypothesis but refuted the distinctiveness hypothesis.  Specifically, we discovered that regional gradients of animacy representation correlated with the number of parts and interconnected relationships of objects but not with the uniqueness of structural features.  Our results indicate that the complexity hypothesis better explains the patterns of animacy representation in the human brain.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader incident, which can significantly reduce the effective value of $R_0$ by a factor of two to the power of two, making it crucial to be understood. To neglect the underlying mechanisms of power-law distributions in population susceptibility and transmission rates would be a significant oversight. A simple yet effective model has been proposed that accounts for a population with inherent characteristics, including a varying transmission rate, and demonstrates how a basic mechanism can result in the occurrence of super-spreader events and consequently, a distributed effective value of $R_0$. The model's predictions have been validated through simulations of a susceptible-infectious-recovered (SIR) epidemic following the power-law distribution of transmission rates, as well as a susceptible-infectious model (SIM) without inherent susceptibility, showing good agreement in the SIM's results. Furthermore, the model's results indicate that a simple quadratic increase in a basic parameter can give rise to the occurrence of super-spreader events observed in real-world data.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a specific type of operator within L(X), to a broader context. Furthermore, we investigate connections between our generalized definition and that of cod cyclicity, providing several relevant illustrations.

The study examined the bi-directional polarimetric data, specifically the
fractional linear polarization and the degree and direction of magnetic field
orientation, obtained through spectropolarimetric observations of the star
ADS 1486 during a specific time frame in 2015 and 2016. By analyzing
ads1486, researchers discovered significant magnetic field variations, both
spatially and temporally, in certain regions, which were identified as
reconnection sites through the comparison of polarimetric and spectral
features. The study also identified several sources of bias in modeling the
component of the magnetic field that is perpendicular to the line-of-sight,
resulting from overlooked effects such as thermal radiation, scattering, and
geometric effects. The investigation revealed that in some areas, the
transverse magnetic field was more prevalent than the component parallel to
the line of sight, which was attributed to absorption of electrons in
regions with high electron densities. The study found that magnetic field
orientation data could be more complex than previously thought, and that
interpretation of results should consider multiple scenarios, such as
inclination effects, to avoid drawing incorrect conclusions. The
ads1486 star's properties were further explored through the analysis of
polarimetric variations, and researchers discovered that the linear
polarization degree was linked to the component of the magnetic field that is
perpendicular to the line of sight

A sign problem has been encountered in Monte Carlo simulations for different fillings beyond a certain point in a localized Anderson model with sign structure, built on a Hubbard-Phonon framework.  We have encountered a much less severe sign problem in these simulations, allowing for larger system sizes and time steps than previously possible.  This is particularly useful in investigating systems with negligible occupation levels, which can be achieved in experimental setups by introducing weak leads.  To tackle this sign problem, we have incorporated the path integral approach and attempted simulations even at different fillings by inserting fermion fields at external points and applying the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to bimolecular terms.  Our results have been obtained using Path Integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) simulations, which have revealed that in systems with large sizes, fermionization forces can overcomes localization and lead to the emergence of bound states on lattice sites.

Let $f$ be a non-erasing free monoid isotopy and $\Omega$ be the set of words for which the words' images under $f$ belong to a subshift $X$. Define $X$-complexity functions $X_f$ and $X$-entropy functions $X_f$ and $X_f$. This paper establishes that the functions $X_f$ and $X_f$ depend only on the isotopy class of $f$ and $\Omega$, respectively, and that the functions and entropies satisfy inequalities involving the functions and entropies of $f$, respectively. Additionally, conditions under which the inequalities become equalities are derived.

By leveraging previously acquired skills, cross-task generalization aims to enable
successful application of learned models in unfamiliar settings.  Due to the
interconnected nature of tasks, this research focuses on enhancing the flexibility
of models across unrelated tasks.  Specifically, we develop the Task-Guided
Generative Pre-training (TGiPT) framework to improve the models' ability to handle
unseen tasks.  In the proposed approach, the model is given the ability to generate
potential training data by appending sentences that match the characteristics of
unseen tasks to the multi-task pre-trained vocabulary.  To effectively accomplish
this, TGiPT employs a two-stage method, combining the benefits of abstract and
concrete task label generation.  As a result, TGiPT achieves notable improvements
in handling previously unencountered classification tasks, and demonstrates
successful applications across two distinct tasks: sentiment analysis and event
detection.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue that has hindered its widespread adoption. Addressing this problem, we explore various parameter-tuning methods under strict privacy constraints, and we compare the performance of established techniques along with a novel set of alternatives. Our research involves a comprehensive evaluation using both synthetic and real-world datasets across multiple machine learning models, and we meticulously document our experiments using the open-source DPSGD framework. Our key findings can be ascribed to the underlying principles of hyperparameter optimization, the characteristics of the data, and the specific machine learning models employed. Our results are publicly accessible through a online resource. Our code is also publicly accessible to facilitate further research and development.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

We applied an advanced statistical model to the radial distribution of twelve key elements in the galactic disk using data from GALAXIA, a comprehensive chemical evolution code. This fast stochastic model was based on the work of Biernacka et al. and utilized two types of supernovae - II and Ia - with their own distinct effects on elemental abundances. The impacts of these supernovae were modeled using nine "prompt" and three "delayed" supernovae components, each with their own associated power law indices. This approach allowed us to examine the relationships between elemental ratios and distance from the galactic center, as well as between elemental ratios and stellar velocities relative to the galactic center. By comparing the results of this model with observational data, we found that it replicated the characteristics of the disk well, and also revealed that the effects of supernovae II and Ia play a significant role in shaping the chemical composition of the galactic disk. This model also provided valuable insights into the dynamics of stellar discs and could serve as a basis for more complex simulations of chemical evolution.

The COVID-19 pandemic spurred the spread of significant health-related rumors online, which can accelerate public panic and harm prevention efforts. This study proposes an improved SIR model that incorporates emotional contagion theory to analyze the combined spread of these rumors and the pandemic. We then derive the basic reproduction number for the model and identify conditions under which the rumors-pandemic system reaches a stable state. Through the construction of Lyapunov functions, we determine the criteria for all system components to converge to their equilibrium points. Additionally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the theoretical findings.

Researchers have frequently utilized extragalactic planetary nebulae to estimate the distances to their associated galaxies. A key factor in this process is the need to understand the relationship between two specific features found in the spectra of planetary nebulae. While previous studies have utilized more complex methods involving multiple spectral indicators, a simpler approach using just one ratio has been used to determine the slope of these spectra and determine their host galaxies' distances. However, recent evidence suggests this approach may be misleading due to the influence of dust on the appearance of planetary nebulae spectra. As an alternative, another method involving multiple spectral indicators was examined to understand the true relationship between the core disks surrounding a planetary nebula and the rest of the surrounding gas. Results from this research show that despite the influence of a surrounding torus, there is a distinct relationship between two specific spectral features in the visible light range. When this new standard is applied to previously observed spectra from within galaxy NGC 1097, it indicates a smaller estimated distance to this galaxy than what was previously determined.

Every day, medical professionals rely on vast amounts of processed physiological data to enhance patient care and conduct research. Although data streaming engines have been used to handle large-scale data processing, the particular requirements of the medical field have prevented the easy deployment of these technologies in healthcare settings. To overcome this barrier, we introduce \emph{LifeStream}, a specialized data processing system built on Apache Flink that efficiently handles physiological data, which typically includes precise time-stamped measurements from devices like ECG monitors and MRI machines. In contrast to existing solutions, LifeStream enables medical practitioners to easily perform real-time data processing tasks on complex physiological data sets, facilitating immediate interventions during critical moments as well as accelerated data analysis for research purposes. By leveraging optimized execution techniques specific to physiological data, LifeStream surpasses the performance of the top-tier Apache Flink benchmark by 1.2 to 2.5 times when processing physiological data sets in a single instance, and achieves up to an order of magnitude better performance when processing datasets across multiple instances. We validate the effectiveness and actual performance gains of LifeStream through various practical examples and large-scale performance evaluations.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function in training a DNN for classified supervised tasks is pivotal, yet determining the most suitable one remains a challenging task due to the vast array of available options. This problem is compounded by the lack of guidance on how loss function performance relates to network architecture and input data characteristics. This situation has led to the common practice of relying on a limited set of loss functions. To address this issue, we present an automated framework that systematically evaluates the performance of various loss functions across multiple dimensions and scales, specifically using a collection of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet networks. By showcasing the significant differences in achieved accuracy among different loss functions in our baseline results, we demonstrate the substantial impact of this choice on network performance. Furthermore, our large-scale analysis reveals that more complex loss functions tend to outperform their simpler counterparts in terms of achieved accuracy.

This research aims to enhance the understanding of strain-induced crystallization in unfilled polymers by incorporating thermal effects and crystallization-induced anisotropy into a model. Originally, the Thomas-Frenkel model was adapted to account for anisotropic anisotropy, and a Gurtin-type non-equilibrium thermodynamics theory was used to establish an anisotropic Thomas-Frenkel model that includes the influence of anisotropy. Furthermore, a supply current was introduced to ensure that the second law of thermodynamics is satisfied, and the resulting equations of thermodynamics were analyzed. Ultimately, an anisotropic supply current was established to comply with the second law of thermodynamics, and the resulting equations of anisotropy were obtained.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields and doping on the p-wave intranode d-wave topological superconductor bi2se3, we investigated its phase diagram using the Ginzburg-Landau theory. Notably, the Meissner effect and the emergence of nematic superconductivity were observed in response to the Lorentz and drag forces exerted upon Cooper pairs, respectively, with these effects being further enhanced by the influence of strong magnetic fields and doping levels. Doping levels, on the other hand, contributed to the expansion of the topological superconducting region while also inducing the Cerny-Dashman transition and a shift in the ratio of the order parameter nodes. Furthermore, we found that the critical field required to induce the Cerny-Dashman force increased with the doping level, with the topological nematic superconductor exhibiting greater resilience to the drag force compared to its intranode d-wave topological superconductor counterpart.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. This robustness makes differential detection a preferred method for implementing conventional CPM demodulation. This work presents the optimal decision rule for differential detection of rectangular Gaussian Minimum Shift Keying (R-GMSK) in vector formats, which consists of two differential symbols, surpassing conventional methods. The proposed method minimizes the probability of error in an AWGN channel, and under certain conditions, it yields the same error performance as the conventional approach, while in other scenarios, it yields a significant improvement. The work also presents an exact asymptotic error expression for the conventional method and compares it with the optimal method, both numerically.

A recent study's findings align with earlier studies and utilize the variance of the free energy, denoted as $f_{ve}$, to assess the variability of energy density around its average value in quantum many-body systems. A key distinction of $f_{ve}$ is its direct correlation with the width of a spectral window in impulse response functions, allowing $f_{ve}$ measurements to leverage existing data without the need for additional experiments. A perturbative analysis of $f_{ve}$ reveals its dependence on relevant coupling constants and allows its expansion in terms of irreducible loops. A comparison with the specific heat shows that $f_{ve}$ shares the same drive for enhancement from both quantum and thermal sources. However, unlike the specific heat, $f_{ve}$ exhibits a more intricate response to spectral features near resonance, offering a complementary perspective on the phase transition in quantum many-body systems. To demonstrate these concepts, we conducted numerical calculations on the quantum Rabi model and the Bose-Hubbard model, extracting relevant parameters from prior studies.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of knowledge, which is free from rewards or spatial relationships, is equipped with associated evaluation values and is complemented by two related datasets that focus on task-oriented actions and spatial relationships.  Actions, which consist of 70,000 text descriptions of news stories and the associated outcomes, is further supplemented with category information, isfer, and a large-scale dataset, eat, which contains nearly ten million text-based descriptions of cause-effect relationships.  We demonstrate through multiple experiments that these datasets are essential for training machine learning models to perform tasks that go beyond object recognition and meal preparation.

The method leverages the HHL algorithm to solve linear equations associated with covariance matrices, achieving a significant speedup compared to the classical approach. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models, we've conducted an in-depth study on the use of synthetic data in a multimodal data-evaluation framework, the Voice3D framework. Our research highlights the difficulty of improving ASL performance with labeled transcribed data and demonstrates the potential of data recycling through the reuse of voice data labels. We found that improving performance with high-quality, labeled text data is particularly challenging. In contrast, results show that 50% more expensive high-resolution audio labels can boost performance, while lower-quality data fails to provide any benefits. Interestingly, using recycled labels in a model trained three times yields the same performance as a single-time trained model with an equivalent amount of initial data. However, our research also indicates that data can be used effectively beyond its original capacity through advanced processing techniques and shows that combining multiple data sets can provide significant improvements over using them separately. Finally, we found that combining our synthetic data with real-world data yields substantial performance gains compared to using high-quality data alone.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, where $k_n$ can be chosen such that it is comparable to $\sqrt{n}$ and where this result holds as $n$ approaches infinity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that asymptotic independence and identically distributed behavior of the first $k_n$ positions, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n))$, do not necessarily imply that $\sqrt{n}$ is the minimum order of magnitude for $k_n$. Notably, we also provide evidence of notable exceptions to this rule and near-critical phases of interest. Additionally, this research extends the parking function model by introducing a new concept of "critical" and "near-critical" phases, similar to those found in random lattice models, and demonstrates that these phases can be significant even when there are only $n$ possible locations, and where we provide precise estimates of how many such locations are required.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, specifically NbN nanowires, demonstrate the connection between the voltage seen during resistance transitions and the critical current, an unexpected finding that has no current explanation. An unanticipated observation, however, is the cause of a conduction blockade in the nanowires, a phenomenon that results from the voltage seen during transition states acting as a feedback mechanism. This, in turn, is linked to a capacity for trapping quasiparticles that has both experimental and theoretical underpinnings.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing methods that rely on narrow angular ranges, our network can generate videos from viewpoints up to 45 degrees, without requiring additional training. A key aspect of our proposed method is its ability to utilize viewpoint-mismatched input videos, without the need for synchronization, and without limiting the angular distance between input and target viewpoints. By employing a simple yet effective design, our proposed network incorporates features from input videos into a prior representation, resulting in novel view video prediction. Our proposed method's superiority over current state-of-the-art novel view video prediction techniques is demonstrated, with quantitative and qualitative results showing notable improvements over baselines.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structures, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, containing sss quarks and having only weak interactions, was theoretically predicted in 1962 but not observed experimentally until 1964 at Brookhaven. A key feature of the R-scalar state, first discovered at CERN in 1979 and later confirmed at Brookhaven in 1999, has long been considered its spin ground state. Nevertheless, recent theoretical studies have highlighted the possible presence of lower-spin states, specifically the 1/2^-, 3/2^-, and 5/2^- configurations, which would have a higher mass than the R-scalar state. An extensive search through the 18-GeV data collected by the BABAR detector for b BΩ pairs has yielded no indications of non-scalar states below 1.8 times 10-tensor sign of the R-scalar state's mass. An extensive fit to the mass distribution has established an upper mass limit of 1.706-tensor sign of the R-scalar state's mass at the 90% confidence level for any possible 1/2^-, 3/2^-, or 5/2^- state.

The spread of virus-causing diseases like COVID-19 is partly facilitated by the transport of aerosols carrying viruses within indoor environments. To effectively prevent their further transmission, it's crucial to understand how these viruses are transported inside buildings. To this end, researchers have used numerical simulations to analyze the transport dynamics of aerosolized viruses. In this review paper, we employ recent simulation data to discuss how air currents move these aerosols indoors. Specifically, we discuss how ventilation systems impact their residence times indoors, how speaking can lead to the infection of listeners in enclosed rooms through acoustic waves, and we discuss strategies to reduce indoor infection rates through ventilation design, changes to ventilation settings, and other measures. This review paper draws on various sources to provide insights and references for readers to explore the topic in greater depth.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect, where a layer adjacent to a strong spin-orbit material experiences enhanced Spin-Orbit Coupling, has both theoretically and experimentally been extensively studied recently. The Topological Side-Affect, resulting in new topological properties, further adds complexity to this phenomenon. These effects, particularly the interplay with long coherence lengths in thin films and semiconductor structures, enable significant control over certain scenarios through SC Josephson junctions and thin film patterns. In this work, we investigate the $0{\pi}$ transitions in STJ's and SC periodic structures due to the spin-orbit coupling, specifically near the interface with the strong spin-orbit layer. We show that this structure exhibits multiple $0{\pi}$ transitions and periodic variations in its properties, leading to unique SC phases, including novel periods with enhanced critical current.

This research examines the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in two dimensions, incorporating the Modified Miura Potential. By performing a variable substitution, the potential takes on a form that allows for the exploration of bound state solutions. Specifically, we analyze a general class of potentials and then focus on a particular form, $V_{1/2}(y) = \frac{\Omega^2 y^2}{4} + \Omega - \frac{\alpha}{y}$, to derive the corresponding wave function. Ultimately, we connect these findings with the well-known harmonic oscillator in fractional contexts.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity with a specific norm can improve its generalization capabilities. Although the ideal approach of training according to this principle is unfeasible, we highlight that adding a regularization term based on the desired norm's value serves as a workable substitute. This method was tested on various neural network architectures and different optimization techniques across multiple benchmarking problems. Experimental data supports the hypothesis that such a regularizer can reduce overfitting and enhance performance. Furthermore, this data is comparable to the results achieved by cutting the training set's size by a factor of ten.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. To accurately perform these calculations, we utilize the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO tool, using a specific type of hypothetical particle known as a "wino leptoquark". We provide detailed code for these calculations and illustrate the corrected predictions through generated data sets, demonstrating the improved accuracy with which these rare particle interactions can be studied experimentally.

Radiation exposure from positron emission tomography (PET) scans can lead to an elevated risk of cancer over time, which is generally considered acceptable given the benefits of PET's diagnostic accuracy. However, its limitations in producing high-quality high-resolution images often necessitate longer scan durations which can compromise patient comfort and movement control. Using shorter scan durations is preferable if any resulting high-rate PET data loss remains within the PET's acceptable range. This study investigates the impact of random data loss due to PET data rejection techniques on the precision of high-resolution images and proposes an assessment method to evaluate the effect of random data loss on scanning efficiency and patient safety. The proposed method leverages the relationship between data rejection and time-resolution to determine how data loss influences image precision and can be utilized to value shorter scan durations for more sensitive patient groups. The proposed assessment can be incorporated into statistical models to value shorter scan durations and aid in selecting optimal scans durations for more sensitive patient groups.

A previous study by Hopper and Traugott highlighted how grammatical elements reflect social cognition, suggesting that syntax and semantics mirror the balance between individual agency and communal norms. This principle can be applied to discourse coherence, as evidenced by linguistic structures that guide attention to relevant information sources. Building on this idea, a framework for analyzing coherent conversations is proposed, utilizing attention-based theories, such as centering theory, which posits that linguistic choices reflect the tension between the speaker's and listener's perspectives. A corpus of coherent and incoherent conversations is used to test this framework, revealing that grammatical choices in incoherent discourse reflect a stronger emphasis on individual perspective. This is evident in the prevalence of passive voice constructions, which attribute actions to actions rather than actors, in the incoherent corpus. These findings have implications for understanding the relationship between language structure and cognition, as well as for developing computational models that can analyze and interpret human communication.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals in buildings. To facilitate this, WiFi infrastructure has been expanded significantly. However, relying on signal strength from mobile devices can result in inaccurate positioning. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel approach using the existing WiFi infrastructure and fixed access points through which signal strength is measured. To position a mobile device, this method utilizes measurements of signal strength obtained from those fixed points. This study compares two positioning positions using installed infrastructure. Both methods were assessed across various datasets and in a practical experiment. Furthermore, this study explores various signal processing techniques to enhance positioning accuracy. To position installed WiFi infrastructure, this study employs a linear regression model. Furthermore, this study employs a deep learning-based approach, specifically a multilayer perceptron, to compare with traditional methods.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators with insertion devices along the ring, potentially limiting the maximum beam current as observed at the Siberia insertion point of the positron ring. A theoretical model is developed to examine how space charge effects influence the BBU development in such scenarios where the effect cannot be disregered, and calculations are performed using parameters from the Positron Ring at the Siberia insertion point.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with arbitrary momenta is derived analytically in terms of scalar integrals, facilitating straightforward numerical evaluation. Notably, the expression consists of four parts: the well-known Wilson line CEV, an additional bulk contribution, and two boundary terms associated with logarithmic corrections to the accuracy.

Theories describing polymer brushes have been developed for flat surfaces and curved structures, providing valuable insights and applications. Despite this progress, the analysis has been limited by the absence of end exclusion zones, which can be resolved experimentally. Our revised theory incorporates these zones into the analysis for various brush architectures, including stars, cylinders, and spherical surfaces. Our method employs self-consistent field theory in conjunction with mean field approximations, revealing significant differences in scaling laws and structural characteristics. The theory indicates that end zones exhibit distinct scaling behaviors on different surfaces and a more disordered brush structure near these zones, which could be verified experimentally or through simulations and neutron scattering experiments.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel application of machine learning image processing techniques to handle data from the Euclid satellite, focusing on using autoencoders to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio in infrared images taken by the Photon and Spectrograph instrument. Since the IR instrument has two sub-instruments, this study specifically addresses one of them, the Spectrograph Instrument, and investigates possible applications for machine learning image reconstruction before its launch. To test this approach, synthetic data was generated and compared with traditional image processing methods, revealing that using machine learning can effectively handle Gaussian noise and results in images with higher signal-to-noise ratios. While using machine learning can lead to improved image quality, this benefit diminishes with lower levels of noise. Furthermore, although autoencoders are versatile and easy to use, they require significant testing to ensure reliable performance in the future.

In response to recent developments in deep reinforcement learning, a significant number of studies have focused on applying combinatorial optimization methods to solve real-world problems and drawing performance comparisons. However, many of these studies lack an analytical framework to draw meaningful conclusions from their experiments and often fail to properly credit established results. We address these issues by examining multiple combinatorial allocation rules, including successful approaches from the literature, as well as novel methods we develop, and present their straightforward descriptions along with relevant findings from the literature through annotated references. Specifically, we analyze several representative studies leveraging deep reinforcement learning and provide a comprehensive overview of their experimental setups, drawing heavily on previously established information. We begin by explaining the problems under consideration, the mechanisms employed, and the reward systems underpinnings of each study, and then summarize their training approaches, hyperparameter configurations, and training procedures, as well as their evaluation procedures. We also provide relevant findings from the studies, both positive and negative, along with notes on their e.g., performance, generalization, and robustness, as well as any proposed interpretations. We also discuss previous approaches related to each study, along with their strengths and weaknesses, and then draw open questions from our analysis for the research community to explore. As a pre-processed resource for the community, we also provide an unannotated reference list for further exploration. We also provide reference sections for each aspect of our analysis, including social welfare, truthful implementation, and more, along with relevant previous approaches,

We designed a novel technique to detect wide binary asteroids by leveraging the conservation of Keplerian energy, suitable for scenarios where binary separation is 10 times greater than the orbital radius of asteroids in shared clusters. Our method was successfully applied to identify and characterize three binary asteroids, 2004 DH48, 2008 TC3, and 2012 TC38, whose bi-naries have extremely wide and previously unexplored parameter ranges. By utilizing our technique on the Space Interferometry Pathfinder (SIP) simulated data, we identified 20 binaries with wide separations within a three-day HST observing window, demonstrating the potential for future missions like LUKE to discover stable binary asteroids and enhance their mass measurements through wide separation measurements, all while making efficient use of limited observing time.

This research extends the prior applications of generalized Residuals and
vAriances (GARCH) models to examine the performance of estimation under varying
conditions. Initially, the current approach differed from the original
GARCH assumptions by modeling not only asset returns but also their corresponding
risks through variable-specific and time-dependent parameters in a simultaneous
equations framework. The prior work and current approach demonstrate how to
estimate this framework through models with individual and combined sets of
variables. Furthermore, the approach evaluates the reliability of results using
simulated data analysis and explores real-world implications through empirical
assessments. The current approach presents econometric analysis showing the
performance of estimation methods in theoretical settings with models subject to
fleeing correlations among multiple variables. Through simulated data analysis,
the approach evaluates the accuracy of various estimation techniques and compares
their outcomes. The approach also presents empirical findings by examining the
individual and collective variables' performance in a real-world context of
global stock markets.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Integral and Derivative with respect to a function. Specifically, we derive first and second Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Product Rules for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Integral and Derivative. We also establish three inequalities of Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Hadamard Algebraic Type. Moreover, we introduce two new identities of Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Chain Rule Type and develop two corresponding inequalities of Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Ratios Type. We further obtain results for Constant-Order Fractional Calculus as special cases. We support our theoretical findings with concise proofs and complement them with r- and t- Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order Fractional Bessel Functions in order to demonstrate the practical applications of these new idenitities and inequalities.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the filter of a human role-player, guided by a Dungeon Master. Using an example from a Dungeons and Dragons game, our preprocessing converts the role-playing game's text into question-answer pairs, tagged with in-game item names. Then, two models work together: one extracts relevant items, and the other ranks them to find the most relevant. Pretraining the model with random tag insertion helps it recognize these tags, significantly improving performance when combined with attention mechanisms. Additionally, a BERT-based guide, initially trained for multi-class classification and fine-tuned with loss reweighting, achieves a 14.3% better score from a human Dungeon Master compared to a baseline.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area of ongoing investigation. Recent research has focused on protein knots not forming true knots, but rather knotoids, which provide a useful modeling tool for understanding their topological and geometric properties. However, existing methods for analyzing their geometry are largely projective in nature. In this research, we present the concept of minimal surface knotoids and establish a surface-boundary relation that holds significant implications for understanding the geometry of 3D projections of minimal surface knotoids, under certain conditions.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A recent interpretation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem, which arises from an anomalous symmetry rather than spontaneous breaking, is supported by the NG-anticommutator's lower bound. This in turn, is a result of an anomalous global symmetry rather than spontaneous breaking. A key implication of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is that it allows for an anomalous contribution to the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, which is also supported by a recent analysis of the neutral pion's mass and its relation to QCD. A possible explanation for the anomalous part of the NG-anticommutator and its connection to the neutral pion could be a possible identification of the NG field with the neutral pion and the anomaly with its axial mass, although this remains an open question that requires a more precise theoretical understanding.

Recent studies have utilized counterfactual examples, data that represents a different classification from the original class but belongs to the same class as the original, to assist in training robust neural networks. Despite these achievements, significantly effort is required to manually create these data points. To address this challenge, our new framework called DISCO counteracts this limitation by automatically producing high-quality data through a data-to-data approach. Our method creates a comprehensive dataset consisting of several alterations from the original data by extracting, modifying, and moving image components, utilizing various data transformation techniques like those in Inverse Graphics Models. By applying this diverse set of augmentations in a controlled manner, we apply our framework to create outputs that match the targets of the new data points, resulting in either the same classification or a different classification from the original. We have demonstrated that applying our method's diverse sets of augmentations in this way allows models trained on its output to generalise effectively.

Researchers have observed that when growing complex compounds like Heusler alloys on graphene, they sometimes see the underlying graphene structure, which could indicate a remote epitaxy process where the compound grows independently of the substrate's crystal structure. To confirm this unusual mode of epitaxy, we looked for specific evidence in characteristics of the deposited layer, such as momentum conservation at domain boundaries, alignment of bonding electrons, and atomic siting above van Hove singularities in the electronic density of states. When growing a compound like Co2MnSi, we found that its reciprocal lattice matches that of the underlying graphene, which is possible due to its high symmetry, but when growing more complex compounds like Co2TaGa or Co2TiSn, we found that their crystal structures align with the armchair or zigzag directions of the graphene, respectively. This is further supported by photoemission spectra showing peaks associated with certain atomic orbitals at specific momentum points, which could be critical for understanding and controlling the growth of these complex compounds in remote epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel for these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the distance of these codes are provided in three distinct scenarios.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, current training methods lack mathematical frameworks for assessing their conditional nature, rendering them susceptible to serving as generative 'oracles' that provide answers without adhering to the intended condition.  We propose a randomization-based evaluation strategy to assess the conditional accuracy of these models, which can also be utilized to guide their training process.  Experimentally, we applied this measure to evaluate and train clothing transformation models based on clothing parts.  Results indicate that incorporating our conditional assessment into the training process leads to improved outputs and more precise fulfillment of target categories.

The GNS construction establishes a correspondence between a state on a C*-algebra and a representation along with a cyclic vector. Traditionally, this process moves from state to representation, but we demonstrate the reverse direction is also feasible for specific cases, particularly when dealing with abelian C*-algebras and their representations allows recovery of the state from the algebra and vector. As an illustration of this principle, we can deduce the famous Riemann-Lebesgue lemma by examining which Hilbert space and cyclic vector appropriately correspond to the characteristic function of an interval within the abelian C*-algebra of continuous functions on the dual of the integers group. Moreover, this approach aligns with the discrete time Heisenberg C*-algebra's characteristic state being the Dirac delta at zero when examined through the same construction, thereby establishing the correspondence between such states and half-norms defined by the algebra's difference operator.

The source catalog from the Fermi-LABS, containing 443 gamma-ray sources between 0.8 GeV and 100 GeV, is used to identify possible targets for future very high energy observations. To do this, we classified the high confidence sources based on their likely origins, categorizing extragalactic sources into galaxies actively shedding mass, bipolar emission patterns, or unknown sources. We found that galaxies actively shedding mass, which includes some starburst galaxies and active galactic nuclei, can be identified within the local universe. To explain the gamma-ray emission observed in these galaxies, a specific range of gamma to proton ratios and proton to electron ratios is necessary. We then proposed a mechanism involving hadronic synchrotron self-absorption that could account for the lack of detected very high energy gamma-ray emissions in some of these galaxies, which exhibit low proton to electron ratios. We also categorised gamma-ray emissions from galaxies with bipolar patterns and unknown sources, before outlining the necessary steps to confirm the extragalactic origin of the GeV gamma-ray sources.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are essential for this purpose.  However, accurately diagnosing heart conditions from auscultation sounds is challenging due to the presence of significant background noise and interference.  To address this challenge and enable effective deep learning models to process raw audio signals, a new training approach is proposed that utilizes spectral amplitude and phase loss functions.  This method is demonstrated on a public dataset containing recorded sounds of normal and pathological heart conditions, and shows an 11% improvement in accuracy for detecting stenosis in heart sounds compared to the current state-of-the-art.

The proliferation of computing technology and connectivity have revolutionized healthcare, enabling continuous, unobtrusive monitoring through wearable devices. Despite these advantages, device usage remains limited due to privacy concerns and data silos, complicating data analysis for meaningful insights. Additionally, the lack of personalized feedback derived from monitored data hinders the devices' utility. To bridge this gap, research has explored leveraging cloud technology to process and generate personalized results on wearable devices. However, this approach is limited by data aggregation and transfer challenges, rendering it unsuitable for many applications. Our research proposes a novel, efficient framework that leverages cloud technology and processed data stored directly on devices, resulting in a breakthrough achievement - real-time health monitoring through devices, continuous data analysis on a cloud platform, and provision of personalized insights, all without excessive data transfer. Our framework utilizes a hybrid edge-cloud architecture, where devices monitor and store data, and the cloud aggregates data, leveraging a data siloage-friendly approach. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a prototype was developed and tested, revealing a 1000x energy efficiency and a 100,000 times speed advantage over existing solutions, while also showing a 95% reduction in data transfer costs.

This research develops a framework for portfolio selection with multiple higher moments, focusing on robust strategies against uncertainties in higher-order portfolio moments. We define a novel class of stochastic programming with higher moments, where we minimize the worst-case distribution of a coherent risk measure under pinned variance constraints for the objective function across various probability measures. Our equivalent deterministic formulation of this problem comprises the original problem plus constraints ensuring the squared returns of assets have consistent variance and covariance under each measure. A new extension of Linear Matrix Inequality, named Pinney Linear Matrix Inequality, is used to characterize this extended problem. Our research also explores explicit solutions for commonly used coherent risk measures, including Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk, and demonstrates numerical applications of our monotonicity and monotone dynamical system properties for PINN.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process that requires careful planning to allocate limited resources effectively and achieve a high-quality outcome within set constraints. This task's stochastic nature and high dimensionality make it an ideal problem for resolving through a combination of simulation and reinforcement learning approaches. We have developed a sophisticated simulation framework and subsequent policy learning method to solve this problem, which includes a realistic simulation of the recruitment process, an application of approximate relative value functions, and a technique for high-dimensional feature extraction based on conditional random sampling. This results in a significant improvement in solution quality compared to conventional planning methods, as demonstrated by a 15-20% enhancement in outcomes across multiple real-world datasets.

This study tackles a complex control issue involving instantaneous costs during regime transitions in a diffusion process, with the option to switch between states voluntarily. The controls considered here cannot decrease the number of states and must meet certain constraints. The primary goal is to determine the cost function that results from optimal controls in this setting. The existence, uniqueness, and regularity of the value function are established, and this is achieved by connecting the problem to a path-dependent stochastic partial differential equation. The relationship to this equation is demonstrated and a comprehensive study of its properties is presented. The research also includes the establishment of representations for the value function through optimal stopping of coupled systems of backward stochastic differential equations. The existence and uniqueness of solutions to this system are proven for systems with both monotone and non-monotone components. The solutions to these systems are found numerically using a four-step method that combines the discrete stochastic pseudo-spectral method and the Crank-Nicolson scheme in time. The solutions obtained numerically satisfy a minimum principle.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how this process can occur, along with its expected yield from the LHC. Although typically negligible, a specific set of scenarios allows for the asymmetric process to outperform the standard one, offering distinct experimental signatures and theoretical insights.

cis-$C_1O$ lines in the farthest galaxy, CIG 55, and found the lines to be asymmetric 
with high-velocity gas detected in the blue wing of these emissions. To understand 
the properties of this gas, we compared our observations with synthetic line profiles 
generated by the GALACTIC code, and estimated the space velocities of the galaxy 
in three-dimensional space. To our surprise, our analysis of the $C_1O$ R(3.8) line 
revealed significant population of lower energy levels in the distant excited 
population of this molecule. To estimate the temperature of molecular gas in this 
galaxy, we developed a two-component model consisting of an LTE and a non-LTE 
population, and found our model to successfully match the observed line profiles 
at a gas temperature of 1000 K and rotation curve matching the observed major axis 
line-of-sight velocity. To estimate the mass of molecular gas in this galaxy, we 
assumed our two-component model to be representative of the entire gas population 
and used the GILBERT code. However, our initial mass estimate was significantly
