The V392 Persei, initially classified as an anomalous I-like nova just 9 years after its discovery, has since exhibited characteristics indicative of later stages of evolution as time passed.  The Nova Observatory Project gathered nearly 4000 spectra over the course of 1.4 years to study the evolution of the system.  The majority of the collected data showed that the peak of the emission from V392 Persei's white dwarf occurred between 6-12 thousand Kelvin and that the associated accretion disk had a much cooler temperature range of 2-6 thousand Kelvin and contributed minimally to observations.  The Emission from V392 Persei quickly cooled down, with the white dwarf temperature dropping within 100 days and the accretion disk temperature within 1 year following the nova's initial eruption.  The accretion disk's minimal contribution to V392 Persei's emission has significant implications for understanding the origins of low mass X-ray binaries.  The collected data also helped V392 Persei's orbital period remain stable, with the collected observations showing that the orbital period remained within a narrow range of 8.967005 +/- 0.000005 days.  The collected data also showed that the collected spectra did not show any signs of a giant planet around V392 Persei.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on the GMM components, assigning one entry to each component's highest probability centroid. Only the component with the closest match to the current user's signal is identified, and the corresponding index is transmitted instead of traditional codewords. This method minimizes data transmission from base station to base station, and offers a tailored codebook for specific users, along with performance evaluation and comparison to conventional coding methods.

A type of natural phenomenon, crosscurrents that occur perpendicular to external forces acting on a grid-like structure, have been observed in various settings, including aquatic environments and atmospheric systems. A study, combined with numerical simulations, examines the robustness of these two-dimensional crossstreams within a three-dimensional system, specifically near the boundaries where they exist. We derive an expression for this stability, indicating that these streams are highly resistant to impurities, provided the lattice meets certain geometric requirements. However, this resistance varies significantly at the edges of the regions where these streams are found. The exact nature of this change is altered if the force acting on the lattice has a one-dimensional or two-dimensional pattern. The positioned and shape of these robust streams are further influenced whether the system is made up of tightly linked or loosely linked grid sections. The Scharfante cell model was used in this research to discover the positional and shape changes. The importance of the grid's connection in defining these streams was further confirmed by an additional model. The 1D and 2D robust streams are further illustrated with simulations of the Glicksberg-Domany system. The findings may have real-world applications in explaining the streams' behavior.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We've examined the potential for binary remnants formed within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) to merge, focusing on binary black holes (BBH), binary neutron stars (BNS), and binary white dwarfs (BWd), based on recent simulations of galactic formation with gaseous, metallic, and stellar components, as well as a detailed analysis of Population III binary evolution. These simulations have evaluated the conditions within NSCs that could lead to the remnant binaries mentioned above, taking into consideration the Kozai-Lidov mechanism and interactions between stars. Our examination has led to the development of a redshift prediction formula for the merger rates of BBH, BNS, and BWd in NSCs. Our findings have shown that a significant portion, approximately 70%, of Population III binary remnants in the form of BWd and BNS will collapse or explode, whereas the majority of BBH will be dispersed by interactions. Our predictions have also been found to be consistent with the observed merger rates of gravitational waves.

In this study, we examine the security risks of a dual hop OFDM system where an intermediate relay passes on a signal to a legitimate receiver. Due to varying channel conditions, some subcarriers may become compromised in various communication hops. To ensure communication security, Subcarrier Allocation and Power Allocation strategies are put in place to maximize end-to-end communication safety. Substantial formulas are developed to characterize communication safety performance, taking into account statistical variations in receiver noise. Algoritmic solutions are also provided to manage subcarriers and signal power for optimal safety performance. Notably, we observe that imperfect secrecy performance at noisy receivers can lead to carrier opportunities and thus impact performance significantly.

Text-based games provide virtual agents with a rigorous platform to evaluate their text generation, comprehension, and decision-making skills.
However, automatic evaluation for these games is limited, relying on simplistic metrics that lack precision and are difficult to apply.
We present a difficult program generation assessment based on precise metrics that are straightforward to calculate, suitable for textual output comparison.
We present how to generate reference answers for the game and how to calculate the metrics automatically.
Also included are examples of the metric calculation process as well as scripts for their automatic computation.

Recent LSTM architecture innovations have significantly enhanced their accuracy, but at the cost of considerable model size expansion. Conversely, certain compression techniques that reduce memory usage by substantial factors, often result in performance declines. Our work introduces two novel LSTM architectures that achieve significant model size reductions through increased component efficiency. Specifically, our models can decrease component size while maintaining performance. Notably, our proposed models can decrease performance expenditure, including the introduction of performance-enhancing components that reduce performance cost. Consequently, our models surpass state-of-the-art results on multiple natural language processing tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, and at the same time, reduce model size. Part of this work was conducted in collaboration with Google.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture within the realm of quantum field theory and anti-de Sitter spacetime can be tested using vacuum state correlations of charged operators. A key insight from this perspective is that the convexity of the spectrum of charges in conformal field theories on AdS should correspond to the vacuum state two-point correlation function exhibiting positive behavior. We propose an alternative, convexity-based criterion for confirming the Charge Convexity Conjecture, particularly for a wide range of theories including free scalar field theories and specific interacting N=4 SYM theories. Although interacting N=1 SYM theories may not meet this criterion due to the massless gluon, the convexity-based condition can still be satisfied in theories with a massive spectrum. The charge convexity's applicability extends to theories with a positive AdS curvature gravitational constant, potentially implying that charged black holes in such theories would exhibit the properties of large charges in the mass sector.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the depth and tight attachment properties of the quotient when divided by the integral power of that ideal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if a specific quotient when divided by the integral power of that ideal has a depth of one, the ring is $F$-rational if and only if the power ideal maintains a depth of at least two for all integers. These findings hold true if the ring is a unique factorization domain and the characteristic is greater than two, under the condition that it has a depth of one. They also hold generally if we examine the quotient with respect to all ideals and assume the ring is Cohen-Macaulay when the characteristic is zero.Generate the meaning of the following symbol in it's appropriate field of study: $H^1$.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy sources and the decline of traditional power plants have led to increased reliance on flexible redispatch measures to balance the grid. To prevent inefficient investments and operational decisions, these measures need to be constrained by cost-effective solutions. However, current market mechanisms, including bidding in balancing markets, often fail to consider this constraint, and instead rely on supply and demand dynamics. Our novel model of coherently coupled markets considers the potential for BCS (Best Cost Standard) to be implemented using flexible options, such as derivatives and contracts for differences. Our analysis reveals that using large orders in redispatch markets can have detrimental effects, leading to potential inefficiencies and unintended consequences. As a result, our findings have significant policy implications, urging caution when restricting order sizes in these markets.

Wamkeve McIntosh's research focuses on wild ramification and differential Galois theory. Specifically, she investigates the behavior of Galois groups under iteration in both fields with rolling characteristics and those containing a characteristic of zero. Her work involves proving that the Galois group for the $n$-th iteration of a generic monic polynomial remains unchanged, regardless of the characteristic's size greater than or equal to two. Additionally, she explores preservation properties of subgroups like stabilizers and resolvents under iteration, proving that their characteristics must roll for them to be subgroups of a resolvent or stabilizer of an iterated function. Her research has significant implications for understanding polynomial iteration and its applications in areas like cryptography.

Saturn's polar atmosphere experiences seasonal variations driven by the tilt of its planetary axis, which results in distinct atmospheric conditions at the north and south poles. Recent observations of Saturn's south pole reveal the formation of broad, warm vortex structures that mirror the features found in the planet's north pole. Although the patterns observed in the south pole exhibit similarities to the north pole, the underlying mechanisms driving these dynamics differ significantly due to the varying amounts of sunlight received by the poles. The interaction between the solar tilt and the planet's own rotation creates unique patterns of jet streams and temperature variations that drive the formation of weather systems. The study highlights the role of thermal circulation in influencing atmospheric features, with implications for understanding the complex interactions between solar tilt, planetary rotation, and atmospheric features on Saturn.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will eventually dissipate and no longer exist beyond a finite time, a result that holds true for solutions that are of Dirichlet type on the boundary and vanish at infinity. A corresponding whole space solution is utilized in this proof. A byproduct of this main finding is the occurrence of the authoring barrier phenomenon for the said exterior problem.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms full symplectic jet bundles of any grade into symplectic Lie bi-differential operators of 2nd order, effectively converting the bundle of n-grade vector fields into a Lie bi-differential operator of 2nd order. This new linearisation functor is shown to be symplectomorphic to the Broucké-Rogers bundle of scalar bi-differential operators of 2nd order, establishing the universality of the former. The symplectic structure for both is explicitly calculated. The development of the full linearisation functor involves the full linearisation bundle of any graded bundle, initially of the form of a graded bundle, and ultimately of a symplectic symplectic bundle of infinite grade after applying the linearisation map. The foundations of the needed mathematics for the above are introduced and discussed.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands and Rallis, or Yang-Baxter equations involving quantum matrices by Aomoto, more naturally within their respective contexts. Consequently, we provide a fresh proof of the quantum Tamagawa numbers for algebraic torus. Specifically, we demonstrate that the density of a certain function involving a quantum determinant with respect to a specific measure equals a quantum volume of a discrete torus. Furthermore, we explicitly describe the measures used and the constant appearing in the equation that follows, for both the quantum determinant and torus.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract information about the properties of matter. Although it's commonly associated with the measurement of intensities, phase information is also crucial in spectroscopy. The importance of phase information is highlighted in this review, with examples drawn from recent publications. The underlying physics of phase-sensitive measurements involving the use of interference between different light-matter interaction pathways is explored, and existing methods that utilize phase information are categorized. In addition, previously unexplored spectroscopic techniques are proposed, including modifications to third-order harmonic generation and Bragg coherent anti-stokes Raman scattering.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures: highly conductive fractures modeled using transmissibility terms and less conductive or completely blocking fractures represented using Dirichlet-Neumann trans interfaces. As an example, we demonstrate the method with four different problems: two involving highly conductive fractures and two involving blocking fractures. Our approach employs low-order Raviart-Thomas elements to approximate Darcy velocities, with fracture conditions enforced selectively on specific pores adjacent to fractures. The resulting non-linear system of equations is efficiently solved using an algebraic multigrid method combined with algebraic Schur-complement techniques.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in scientific discovery, particularly in areas where new findings are uncovered. Traditionally, Bayes factors have been employed to assess hypotheses, yet their calculation largely relied on the importance sampling technique. This re-examination introduces two innovative methods based on composite Neumann series to calculate Bayes factors and control variance effectively by reducing the composite precision. Through multiple test cases, including the Cosmic Microwave Background and Higgs boson scenarios, the lower variance performance of these methods is demonstrated, surpassing the composite Neumann series with a single-precision component and the existing control variance techniques like balanced Bayes factors and prior predictive matching. This study also features novel simulations of the Higgs bosation and Cosmic Microwave Background that will be made accessible to the public.

Discourse indicators like "actually" and "then again" hint at underlying connections between statements, yet current computational models of language lack the capacity to account for these nuances. We investigate how machines can automate the classification of such words, utilizing pre-trained language models and a customization technique called label noise robust training to handle the subjective nature of this classification task. This method is assessed on two datasets, showing a significant enhancement in performance compared to standard approaches, and also revealing that discarding ambiguous instances can substantially boost the efficiency of these models.

We investigate a common manifold structure across generalized matrix decomposition methods, specifically by studying a highly specialized form of matrix factorization. We establish a global landscape across a Riemannian quotient space defined by the unique geometric properties of the Burer-Monteiro method, and investigate the relationship between the original landscape and a simplified landscape for rank-reduction methods with orthogonal equivalence symmetry. We then analyze a wide range of matrix factorization methods, including those used in variational autoencoders and non-negative autoencoders, on this Riemannian quotient geometry and identify a global landscape with three distinct regions. Under certain conditions, we find that stationary points from the original Burer-Monteiro landscape correspond to those on the simplified Riemannian quotient geometry, and that optimal solutions are isolated. Numerical experiments on variational autoencoders and soft-ITCR demonstrate that optimized matrixes maintain low-rank properties and that the original and simplified landscapes share the global optimal solution. Our study provides a geometric understanding of various matrix factorization methods, and offers a strategy to manage optimization landscapes for more complex methods.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms within a binary game framework, where agents were modeled by artificial life forms with socio-learning and self-interest components. Our findings revealed that using artificial life forms led to a more rapid and reliable convergence to a Nash Equilibrium when agents engaged in socio-learning, both individually and collectively, in contrast to the consistency required by self-interest learning alone. Our results further supported the notion that the combination of artificial life learning and payoffs led to a more stable identification of Nash Equilibrium, in contrast to the oscillatory behavior observed when using payoffs individually. Our study also demonstrated the reliability of using artificial life learning as a means to model the combination of artificial life and payoffs.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and a prime ideal $P_i$ associated with each of its edges $e_i$. This setup allows us to define two power variants for each edge and collectively, for the edge ideal $I$ of $\mathcal{D}$, with corresponding power variants $I^{(r)}$ and $I^[r]$ for each natural number $r$. In this work, we establish that if certain directed paths do not exist within certain subsets of the directed paths of $\mathcal{D}$, then the ordinary and symbolic power variants for $I$ will coincide. Additionally, we provide several examples and characterize a specific class of weighted directed trees where the ordinary and symbolic power variants for $I$ will also coincide for any power.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like autonomous vehicles and surgical robots. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying computational components, including GPUs, against potential faults. This study examines two potential error scenarios: bit flips in GPU memory and GPU functional faults, and investigates activation clipping as a possible mitigation strategy. Activation truncation limits the magnitude of activation values entering nonlinear functions to prevent incorrect results from affecting the final output too significantly. This study evaluates activation clipping's effectiveness in containing errors, subject to certain constraints, and explores optimal clipping thresholds to minimize the probability of incorrect classifications. A novel recognition pipeline is also proposed to detect errors in GPU deployments by analyzing the distribution of classification results and comparing them to a reference model trained on error-free data. This pipeline can identify errors, alert to their presence, and alert to their possible types.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version known as the $(\alpha, \beta)$-extended Jordanian twist. This generalized version meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle condition within the algebra of polynomials involving two variables. Additionally, we have determined how it modifies the co-commutator operation.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages. Our innovation lies in aligning vocabulary spaces across different languages based on their respective common-sense meanings, thereby allowing for easy transfer of meanings and assumptions across languages. We extract three distinct types of data - clustering features based on word contexts, word embeddings, and named entities - from monolingual resources. These data serve as frameworks for grouping words within each language. We then refine the alignment of vocabulary spaces across languages through a cooperative minimization of distances between corresponding clusters. Next, we apply a mapping process to connect words to their respective clusters, and subsequently transfer labels, entities, and names from high-resource to low-resource languages. Our methodology shows substantial advancement over current multi-language semantic alignment techniques, achieving a 10.8% enhancement on the SemEval 2013 dataset without relying on parallel corpora or annotated data from the target language.

The initial production of particles in high-energy collisions is believed to be influenced by the collective behavior of the generated matter. A key characteristic used to describe this radial flow is the slope of the transverse momentum distribution of generated particles. A study was conducted across various collision types and energies, from proton collisions to heavy ion collisions at different energies, to examine the relationship between radial flow and the total number of produced particles. The study found that, after normalizing for collision energy, there is essentially no connection between radial flow and the total number of produced particles when analyzing heavy ion collisions at lower energies. This lack of connection becomes more pronounced as the produced particle count increases beyond a certain point, corresponding to when the generated matter reaches the state of quark-gluon plasma. This observation calls into question using the generated particle count as a universal metric for tracking the size of the produced system in high-energy collisions.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances swept through much of Chile's capital, Santiago. To better understand the geography of these riots, researchers analyzed social media data from Twitter to create a detailed map of the affected areas. By combining this data with information on Santiago's population and transportation routes, they identified four key influences shaping the spread of violence: the city's existing infrastructure, demographic patterns, and a "bandwagon effect" where participation fueled further engagement, all amplified by Santiago's subway system. Surprisingly, this study found that Santiago's geography behaves similarly to self-organized critical systems seen in nature, rather than being primarily shaped by underlying geographic features.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, going beyond traditional approaches which struggle with expressions that reference other parts of the same expression, a common limitation in applications like web document verification and biosequence annotation. We introduce a general algorithm for solving the containment problem with extended regular expressions, which refer to themselves, and specify polynomial time methods for smaller polynomial degrees, specifically O(|P|^ 3) and beyond. The derived algorithms can also be used to address other problem variants, including language comparison and recognition, and imply corresponding solution methods for equation systems matching the criteria for regular expressions that describe languages with expansion rules.

Mobile agents require accurate and reliable positioning, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate how agents move by combining data from cameras and inertial measurement units (IMUs). These systems process vast amounts of information simultaneously, and to handle this challenge, machine learning methods have been explored. However, the potential of generative models in making these algorithms efficient has not been fully utilized. In this research, a novel approach based on the conditional connectionist LLM for VIO, utilizing attention mechanisms to filter out superfluous data, is proposed. This method leverages a generative framework, initially trained with an intermediate representation, and refines the agent's trajectory prediction by employing the same attention mechanism to identify and remove redundant information. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the CGLLV-MV2 estimator was developed, which employs the conditional LLM part based on the MViT backbone and the conditional LLM part to process high-frequency IMU data. This research shows that by leveraging such model components and assumptions, complex VIO systems can successfully manage the high computational demands they face.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layers, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the existence of hinge states and fermi-arcs. Notably, our theoretical model can be physically realized using near-degenerate optical modes, thus bridging the gap between the SHOWS concept and its real-world application.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to approximate the solutions numerically, and both theoretical and graphical convergence results with varying grid resolutions are provided. Furthermore, the robustness of the method is showcased through various test scenarios.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) approach, a method that allows participating entities to join the training of a distributed model without revealing their data to the leader entity managing the model. FedSA is a flexible, flexible, and efficient implementation that provides scalability, simplicity, and data privacy for participants. FedSA models are trained on disparate datasets and can be applied across various model types and data sets. To validate its effectiveness, we conducted experiments using four different models and datasets, comparing FedSA with traditional training and two leading privacy-preserving techniques. The results showed that FedSA achieves performance on par with traditional training and surpasses the privacy-preserving methods, while also being more efficient and scalable than its counterparts.

We examine how elliptic curves defined within the rational numbers behave when extended into degree 4 fields, specifically those with Galois groups of $S4$ and $A4$, focusing on the rank growth between the original and expanded fields.

A crucial boundary condition in physics is represented by the quantum null energy condition (QNEC), which limits the extent to which the energy-momentum tensor can exceed zero. Utilizing entanglement entropy as a measure, a new approach is proposed to analyze the quantum inequalities that arise from field theory and gravity, bypassing traditional methods such as field theory correlation functions, optical theorems, and field displacements. Instead of relying on dynamical equations, this method derives the connection between entanglement and inequalities, which includes the famous Bekenstein bound, covariant Holographic Entanglement entropy (HEE) principle, quantum inequalities, and the quantum inequalities of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC) and the quantum focusing conjecture (QFC). Furthermore, by applying this method to free scalar field theory, verification is obtained of the entanglement-based origin of the quantum inequalities, demonstrating that the entanglement entropy of a free scalar field adheres to the quantum inequalities, including the quantum null energy condition (QNEC) and the quantum focusing conjecture (QFC). As a result of this discovery, the covariant Holographic Entanglement (HEE) principle and the quantum focusing conjecture (QFC) are also validated, and the quantum inequalities can be viewed as inherent properties of the entanglement entropy. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a non-zero probability. This condition enables us to upper bound the distinguishability time for any qubit state under unitary dynamics, and notably, initial states with minimal asymmetry demonstrate extended times before they can be detected. We also apply this criterion to several typical processes of information erasure and compare their times to the upper bound, and find that unitary dynamics that minimize the time can lead to a fundamental limit on state distinguishability, and thus unitary evolution, and consequently, information creation, and is found to be proportional to $\hbar$ times $2\Delta E/h$, where $\Delta E$ is the energy spread of the spectral components.

Consider a unit cube in n-dimensional space, denoted as $Q_n$. Let $C(Q_n)$ represent the set of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$, with the norm defined as the maximum absolute value of a function at any point in $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1^n$ and $\Pi_m^n$ be the sets of trilinear polynomials in $\mathbb{R}[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ up to degree $m$ in each variable. This study focuses on determining the constants of best approximation for the unit and bi-unit balls when restricted to the subspaces $\Pi_1^n$ and $\Pi_m^n$, with respect to the sup-norm.

Superconducting quantum circuits are rapidly becoming an important platform for quantum computing. To achieve scalable applications, it is essential to address material flaws that cause decoherence at connected quantum register interfaces. We developed a technique using nanofabricated capacitive networks as tuning elements in superconducting quantum circuits. By integrating networks with distinct nanofabrication features, we found that they provide different capacitances as expected. Moreover, we utilized these networks to adjust the frequency of a quantum register component to match another component, resulting in high-fidelity state transfer between them. The state transfer achieved greater than 99% fidelity, and the scaling of the networks was verified with minimal dielectric loss. This study provides a efficient and low-loss tuning method that can address material flaws and enable scalable superconducting quantum processors.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, focusing on how its gaseous components changed over time and how these changes relate to the planet's present conditions. Understanding the processes that shaped the atmosphere is crucial, as they reflect on underlying geological and surface properties of the planet. We utilized a one-dimensional global climate model and a two-reservoir atmosphere-ocean evolution model to examine the atmosphere's history, considering both its internal consistency and mass balance. The study reveals significant shifts in atmospheric composition throughout the planet's history. Initially, CO2 levels were around 10^-2 to 10^1 times the current values, with H2O making up 50-90% of the gaseous component. As volcanic activity waned, a runaway greenhouse effect was triggered, raising surface temperatures to over 380 K and evaporating surface water. This led to space loss of hydrogen, a decrease in humidity, and an increase in CO2 levels. The model and mass balance approach converge on similar outcomes, with estimates of volcanic activity falling within a range of 0.1 to 10^10 W.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as volcanic eruptions, heartbeats with abnormalities, or online forum posts, are crucial for modeling event-type data. In this view, predicting the next event involves estimating its type and occurrence time based on previous events. We have developed a novel modeling technique, the multitype causal influence Hawkes process, which estimates both the preceding events of a specific type and their direct impact on future events of that type. This approach is particularly valuable for data mining and can help identify previously unknown event connections and their impacts. We have demonstrated the process's ability to model certain types of data and its potential for forecasting future events of a specific type, such as predicting upcoming earthquakes using historical seismic data.

We have developed a concept for an ultrafast, large-scale plasma waveplate that can instantly change the power supply of a high-energy laser. It uses a Gaussian profiled plasma layer to transform circularly polarized light to linearly polarized light, effectively doubling the output power without losses, as theoretical calculations and time-dependent Schrödinger Maxwell simulations have validated. However, although initially effective at a specific wavelength and plasma density distribution, this plasma waveplate is not adaptable to different parameters and requires precise control, as even minor deviations from the target conditions can significantly reduce its efficiency and cause reflection of the input light.

Re-examining the search for a non-zero electric dipole moment in the tau lepton, denoted by the form factor $d_\tau$, involves studying the process $Z \to \tau^+\tau^-$, where a tau lepton decays into a muon, a muon neutrino, and an antineutrino, and the other tau lepton decays into hadrons plus a $D^0$ (or $\bar{D}^0$), which then produces a visible $K_S^0$ along with other hadrons. By utilizing the angular distribution of final-state particles in such processes, both of which originate from $\tau$ decays, and considering analyses that leverage visible $K_S^0$ candidates to categorize events, unusually, using information from both $\tau$ decays to enhance sensitivity, we define three relevant $d_\tau$ sensitivities. In a purely hadronic scenario for the $\tau^0 \to hadrons + \nu_\tau$ decay, these are estimated to be $4.8 \times 10^{-17}~e\cdot cm$ and $6.4 \times 10^{-17}~e\cdot cm$ for $Z \to \tau^+\tau^-$, using ATLAS and CMS datasets corresponding to 100 $fb^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, respectively. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario.

Building on previous work by \cite{Fitzgerald, Li, LiLiSong}, we developed novel integral representations for OPE block components corresponding to spinning primary fields, extending beyond the dipole component. Through verification via Ward identities, we confirmed that these representations accurately replicate the CFT's response to specific perturbations. Furthermore, through the application of bulk-to-boundary and double-trace to double-trace transformations, we were able to recover known results for CFT response fields associated with the free scalar field, Friedman's field, and a cubic cubic coupling coupling field to two currents.

In 1994, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo during its early stages using the 1.5m GTC telescope at the Calar Alto Observatory. SN~2020jfo, a bright Type II supernova with a peak absolute magnitude of M_V = -18.3, was first observed just 0.5 days after its emergence. The supernova's bright and long-lasting H-alpha emission, with an absolute magnitude of M_5007 = -16.6, indicates a proton star or neutron star as its core. The SN's spectrum initially showed a lack of broad helium emission, a common feature in most Type II supernovae, but this feature appeared around 12 days after its onset. The SN's progenitor mass, estimated to be between 9 and 15 times that of the Sun based on constraints from its light curve, line emission, and line absorption features, places it on the higher end of the range for typical Type II supernovae. The SN's line emission and line absorption features, a rare occurrence, are also discussed in detail.

To significantly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors based on lobster-eye optics, we propose a concept of multiplexing independent fascicles. By utilizing fast phase-shaping mirrors, we can combine multiple subunits into one output of a lobster-eye array. Although this approach does not provide focal localization for detected photons, it allows us to detect sudden events in our wide field of view and then reconfigure the array to focus its output onto the relevant image sensor for detailed event analysis. We explore various mirror control patterns to create unique trigger responses from the array and present a hypothetical application of space situational awareness with dynamic focalization capabilities.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning approach was used, employing hierarchical models to predict the distribution of dark matter halos from either spatial data or including the velocity information in the predicted data sets. Multiple simulation sets were tested to verify the results, each with different characteristics of initial fluctuations and different halo mass scales within the predicted data sets. Various prediction models were compared to ensure the findings were widely applicable. The results showed that predicting halos based solely on dark matter data was possible, but adding velocity information narrowed the halos distribution, especially when tested in different initial conditions and halo mass scales. The influence of velocity on the halos mass prediction is inherent, unprompted by the trained model, and halo shape predictions were also made based on dark matter data sets. The including velocity information was most effective in a specific range of halos, corresponding to those with an average spherical distribution.

We have developed a novel approach to constructing equilibrium configurations of rotating stars under general relativity, utilizing a Lagrangian formulation that tracks fluid elements from an initial state to steady rotation. This methodology enables us to directly solve for stellar metrics and verify key conservation laws, such as mass and angular momentum, while preserving coordinate labels for individual fluid elements throughout the process. 

By integrating this Lagrangian approach with a perturbation expansion in angular velocity, we have successfully modeled the transition of a non-rotating stellar configuration into equilibrium states under slow rotation, characterized by frame-dragging effects and centrifugal forces. This allows us to utilize simple initial conditions and obtain precise equivalencies between fluid element coordinates and perturbation parameters, ultimately facilitating the calculation of gravitational waveforms generated by rapidly spinning stars through fluid element tracking.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, while only marginally reducing performance.

The collaboration between the LIGO and Virgo detectors has enabled the identification of three distinct types of compact binary mergers: binary black hole collisions, collisions between neutron stars and anything else, and the merging of neutron stars with other celestial bodies. Each of these events generates precise data on their masses, distances from Earth, and other characteristics, which can be used to construct catalogs that support the development of astrophysical models. We present a Bayesian approach to infer properties of populations from these events by combining the details of individual events with broader categories based on observable characteristics that may reflect physical processes beyond what's measurable directly. This method offers the flexibility to incorporate both directly and indirectly obtained data while also accounting for events that may go undetected. Furthermore, it can be applied to various areas of research, such as understanding the environments in which black holes are formed, estimating how often they occur, and analyzing the relationships between event properties and events themselves. This approach is illustrated through the use of electromagnetic signals from neutron star mergers, which can be used to determine the properties of the environments in which they occur, such as the density of the universe at those points in time when these events occurred, and how this information can be used to better understand the events themselves.

The urban landscape is characterized by numerous simultaneous interactions between people and objects, from casual encounters that spur innovation to intricate logistics for delivery services. The collective impact of these micro-level events significantly influences the economic productivity of cities and global supply chains. Despite their prevalence and significance, fully simulating their collective influence on the economy and supply chains remains elusive due to the vast number of variables and constraints involved. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach using agent-based modeling and graph theory to model the relationship between the physical and digital realms. By leveraging ABM's micro-simulation capabilities and graph theory's systemic perspective, we can capture the intricate feedback loops between physical encounters and digital data that drive the economy and supply chains. The result is a powerful framework for analyzing and forecasting the dynamics of urban landscapes and supply chains, enabling us to understand how small-scale physical interactions influence large-scale economic and logistical outcomes.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects, which then fall back onto the star in distinct episodes.  The characteristics of these accretion bursts are heavily influenced by the distribution of objects in the system, as well as by asymmetries in their velocities and spatial orientations.  As a result, the relationship between observed variability and that of other observational attributes becomes complex and non-linear.  Notably, the variability observed in the far-infrared and submillimeter wavelengths may not accurately reflect the behavior of accretion in high-mass young stellar objects.  Furthermore, the timing of the most intense variability observed in these objects may not coincide with the largest accretion bursts occurring at their cores.  As such, any theoretical models aiming to explain their variability must take into account the object distribution and asymmetries present in their systems.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with non-zero constant vorticity. Using the Kirchoff-Helmholtz variable, both deep and intermediate depth fluid flows are effectively modeled. We focus on the implementation of the Kirchoff-Helmholtz variable for intermediate depth flows and model the effect of flow using a linear equation. Through a nonlinear multiple scales expansion, we derive the modified nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, which accounts for the influence of non-zero vorticity. Our analysis reveals how flow strength and direction, as well as water depth, impact the modulational instability of wave packets. Our analytical findings are corroborated by direct numerical simulations of the modified nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

In complex and unpredictable environments, navigation tasks often require the robot to navigate successfully despite adverse conditions, limited or unreliable sensors, and unexpected situations. In such scenarios, it is crucial to continue navigating successfully in changing and unpredictable conditions, even when the surrounding conditions may be difficult or unexpected, and where the robot's sensing equipment may be limited or unpredictable. Real-world conditions can be harsh and unpredictable, and in such cases, the robot's sensory equipment may fail, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be limited or unpredictable. In this paper, we present a general framework that enables a robot to continue navigating successfully in harsh and unpredictable conditions, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be difficult or unexpected, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be limited or unpredictable. Our framework combines a deep reinforcement learning-based navigation policy with a safety net that ensures safe navigation when the robot's sensory equipment may be difficult or unexpected, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be limited or unpredictable. Our framework is evaluated in simulation and real-world conditions, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be difficult or unexpected, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be limited or unpredictable. Our results show that the framework enables a sensorless robot to navigate successfully in harsh and unpredictable conditions, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be difficult or unexpected, and where the robot's sensory equipment may be limited or unpredictable.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue, but rather one that's been exacerbated by the ease of access to news through social media platforms. To investigate how effectively large language models can detect false news, we manually verified 2000 YouTube videos and associated Reddit posts from two prominent political figures to ensure our dataset's accuracy. Our dataset, called FALSO, consists of securely checked transcripts, along with metadata such as view counts and dates, and was made available to participate in a benchmarking tournament where multiple LLMs were evaluated on their ability to identify false news. The results of this assessment, which showed surprisingly low performance by the participating models, prompted us to analyze the reasons behind this poor performance and to explore possible solutions. One such solution, called LLM-FALSE, incorporates an external knowledge component by retrieving and incorporating metadata into the models' training, which showed significant improvements in the detection of false news across multiple benchmark tests.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these models, the geometry of a manifold derived from the Fisher information matrix, to better understand the underlying principles of the models. The theory examines how the geometry changes in response to various inputs, and through numerical simulations, the approach is applied to analyze the models' behavior over time and space. The results show that as the models are manipulated, the manifold's structure adjusts, providing a visual representation of the models' adjustments and adjustments in the models' parameters. The study also reveals that the models can detect and adapt to changes in the environment, including sudden shifts and periodic patterns. The information extracted from the models can be used as a input for other models, such as reinforcement learning, to learn the models' patterns. The approach is demonstrated using numerical examples, and the code is made available online for others to use and build upon.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been shown to be a more effective alternative to conventional PCA (Lp norm with p equals 2). Unlike PCA, L1-PCA optimization is not differentiable and results in a non-smooth problem. To address this challenge, a new iterative reweighted algorithm has been developed, leveraging the connection between a specific variant of PCA and a partial isometry problem. By exploiting this relationship, the algorithm efficiently solves an update subproblem through iterations that preserve the rank of matrices, thus maintaining computational feasibility. Numerical experiments have demonstrated that this proposed method outperforms existing solutions, such as COCV and LAPACK, in both speed and accuracy.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that, when applied, can guide the annotation process with labeled data. This study, which employs BERT, a neural language model, in an iterative process combining machine learning and active annotation on a corpus of dialog transcripts, yiealds a modest performance boost of 10 percent compared to unenhanced annotation using standard annotated test sets. Furthermore, the study provides a detailed account of the annotation process and yields valuable insights for future research.

For mobile robots to navigate in unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective and suitable mapping system is essential. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on point clouds, which demand substantial computational resources, particularly for real-time applications. We present a resource-efficient alternative by combining semantic information from a mobile robot's sensors with its occupancy grid map. This method leverages object segment labels obtained through an instance segmentation model trained on static objects, providing a computational-efficient solution. Our proposed OSAM, or Object Semantic Attention Map, utilizes these object segment labels to enhance the occupancy grid map's representational power. A attention mechanism is employed to integrate semantic information from various objects, emphasizing relevant components for each cell. Object segment labels from multiple instances both within and beyond the robot's immediate reach contribute to a localized map representation. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through simulation and real-world experiments, showcasing significant improvement over a non-attention-based encoding approach while maintaining low computational cost.

One of the primary challenges in metrology is accurately measuring very small fractions, such as the minimal amount of magnetic flux that can be expelled by a superconductor. The Meissner effect, which causes a superconductor to expel magnetic fields, is relevant here. We suggest an experimental method to measure the flux quantum precisely, utilizing NMR techniques to detect the subtle inclination induced by expelled flux on a strongly magnetized Gaussian spin ensemble. The sensitivity of this method is driven by the substantial NMR frequency shift induced by even a tiny inclination and the subsequent signal amplification through signal ensemble recycling. The accuracy of this technique relies on correctly modeling the relationship between the superconductor and the sample's geometry, which can be achieved using numerical methods. This approach offers a way to attain high precision, as the method's core components - NMR, dynamic decoupling sequences, and quantum locked amplification - enable operation well within their noise floors, and it avoids direct detection of the minute magnetic field around the sample.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques have been developed to assess the number of components and to identify the aspects of components that are unaffected by noise. The impact of noise on identifiability and the relationship between the amount of data collected and the difficulty of identification were also examined theoretically. Furthermore, difficulty measures were proposed and one specific algorithm was analyzed with regard to its performance. Results showed that in certain signal-to-noise conditions, only the spaces affected by noise cannot be uniquely determined, while other spaces can be determined with a data amount that is significantly lower than in the absence of noise. In scenarios where conditions are not met, even basic properties cannot be identified and difficulty measures were used to quantify them. The difficulty analysis involved examining the relationship between difficulty and various parameters, such as the amount of noise, admixture proportions, and the amount of data collected.

High-performance computing (HPC) applications often involve multiple data types, and optimizing them using only a single programming method is both time-consuming and challenging. To address this, the authors developed an alternative approach that combines deep learning and traditional optimization techniques, and applied it to optimize the GPR solver in PETSc. By leveraging the GPR solver's interface, they were able to tune the GMM solver, resulting in a 1.8x speedup in SMMO SMMO (Single-Method Multiple-Objects) simulations using HYPRE. Furthermore, by exploiting the GPR solver's intercept mechanism, they achieved a 20% speedup in SIM (Single-Method Single-Object) simulations using PETSc's native interface. These achievements were made possible by utilizing hybrid data structures and custom operators to reduce memory consumption and enhance cache efficiency.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This framework relies on an accurate description of local magnetic and spin-orbit interactions within a self-consistent method. Specifically, we applied this framework to N impurities situated on the surface of lead, utilizing the tight-binding approach. Our calculations employed various values for the exchange interaction ($U$) and spin-orbit coupling ($\Delta_{soc}$), and examined the influence of varying $N$ from 2 to 100 with impurities spaced 12 lattice units apart. The comparison between calculated and experimental data for the exchange interaction yielded the most accurate results. Notably, we discovered a robust correlation between the local density of states and the binding energy of the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov state for each of the impurities. Furthermore, we identified a pressing need to re-examine the relationship between the local density of states and magnetism in certain experimental setups.

The NASA TESS mission's launch in April 2018, with its expansive 42 square degree field of view, covers roughly one tenth of the sky observed by the K2 mission, granting a fresh opportunity to study the formation and development of short-period planetary systems in our local neighborhood. Although the TESS data will primarily serve future research on planetary systems located in the lower magnitude range beyond the nearby stars within the TESS field of view, it also offers a unique opportunity to investigate the typical evolution of young planets within the first billion years of their existence in the closest star systems. We have compiled TESS light curves for 1,034 nearby (d < 50 parsec) young stars (ages < 1 Gyr) not previously included in the DISC catalog and have identified 14 transiting planets and brown dwarfs associated with these stars. We have also compiled a list of 1,404 candidate systems for further investigation. We have specifically gathered brown dwarf and planet occurrence rates within the closest 50 parsecs, where external forces like tidal interactions and radiative forces may have a substantial impact on their evolution. We have also compiled a catalog of exoplanets located within the TESS field of view and have compiled a list of protoplanets and brown dwarfs found within the L90 volume.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2 using a first-principles approach.  Calculations showed that when carbon or nitrogen replace titanium atoms, they behave nonmagnetically, and this behavior is linked to the strong hybridization between their $2s$ and $2p$ orbitals.  Additionally, deep electron localization was observed for the impurity states.  On the other hand, when these elements replace oxygen atoms, they exhibit magnetic properties due to weaker orbital interaction and electron localization.  Specifically, nitrogen in a substitutional oxygen site exhibits a higher formation energy and deeper electron localization compared to carbon in the same site.  Furthermore, carbon exhibits higher magnetism and shallower electron localization than nitrogen when substituting an oxygen atom.  These findings are supported by optical absorption spectra calculations.

This letter describes the initial investigation of the likelihood that the production of top-quark pairs can be tagged in two directions at the Large Hadron Collider through the emission of radiated protons. Calculations were performed utilizing effective field theory and matrix elements containing two soft or radiated protons, considering two hypotheses concerning interacting components of proton states. Calculations indicate that, at 13 TeV energy, a specific configuration with two tagged protons emits approximately 16 top-quark pairs per femtometer-cubed, providing a valuable marker for identifying the scattering process free from background interference.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits rather than qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become feasible with near-term hardware using qutrits, achieving the same accuracy using qubits could be challenging and might require access to a device with thousands of qutrits rather than just tens of qubits.

Research indicates that positrons, which can be generated through interactions between lasers and solid materials, exhibit a notable level of polarization. A computational model was employed to analyze the polarization of these positrons as a function of the incident laser's intensity, with the model incorporating various factors such as target geometry, plane-wave approximation, and the role of vacuum fluctuations. Although the model's results provide initial insights, they are limited in accuracy and applicability, highlighting the need for more precise and comprehensive investigations using realistic methods and samples. Furthermore, understanding the underlying mechanisms driving positron polarization can lead to enhanced control over produced polarization levels and offer valuable insights into the behavior of quantum spin in charged particles accelerated by intense electromagnetic fields.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of at most n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup whose size is comparable to that of the most significant abelian part of the group. This is relevant to an open question in computational mathematics concerning the efficiency of expressing elements of specific classes of groups, such as graph groups, as products of a fixed set of elements.

This research develops a fully integrated CMOS temperature sensor, featuring a temperature-to-digital converter with a range of 0 to 100 Celsius and utilizes a linearized PTAT (proportional to absolute temperature) circuit for precision measurements. The system includes an adaptive voltage and frequency scaling controller that adjusts based on temperature readings. The controller dynamically modifies supply voltage and core clock frequency in response to temperature changes within the 0 to 100 Celsius range. The adaptive circuit was fabricated using a 0.18-micron CMOS process, consuming just 1.2 milliwatts at 3.3 volts, with dimensions of 1.02 millimeters by 1.02 millimeters. Experimental measurements demonstrate that the VDD sensor accurately tracks temperature changes with an average error margin of 4 Celsius over the specified range, whereas the FREQ sensor exhibits larger deviations with a frequency error up to 20 percent. The provided VDD sensor and FREQ sensor designs can be incorporated into DVFS (dynamic voltage and frequency scaling) systems to enhance their adaptability.

This doctoral research focuses on exploring the connection between gauge fields over Lie groupoids and their associated algebraic structures, specifically Chern-Simons forms and their derivatives within the context of principal bundles. A Lie groupoid serves as an intricate framework that encapsles various mathematical concepts, including groupoids, manifolds with symmetries, and folded manifolds. A principal bundle over such structures involves compatible collections of bundle data and ischries transformations. We will examine how suitable curvature forms arise as differential forms with a 2-cocycle structure, exhibiting compatibility properties analogous to Banderer's twisted bundle in a case with an intricate symmetric configuration. The Chern-Weil map is also investigated, demonstrating its behavior as a nonlinear evaluation form in association with bundle-associated collection data's characteristic classes. This exploration reveals that resulting characteristic classes possess intricate symmetric and folded symmetries, accompanied by twisted bundle data and Ising's twisted bundle data.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores in the infrared dark clouds of TMC-1/1612 and Serpens South/329 was conducted, with a distinction made between protostellar and starless cores based on detected point sources, as summarized in a table for each cloud.  In TMC-1, the serendipitous nature of the observations using the ALMA array led to the potential bias towards more massive cores with detectable emission, although the core masses still spanned a broad range from 0.5 to 15 solar masses.  In contrast, the Serpens South observations using the ALMA local configuration enabled the detection of a broader spectrum of core masses from 0.5 to 5 solar masses and even allowed for the identification of very low mass cores in the core catalog.  In both clouds, the core mass distributions of protostellar and starless cores exhibited similar trends, with the majority falling between 1 and 10 solar masses and a lack of low mass cores below 0.5 solar masses.  Infrared dark clouds appear to give rise to prestellar cores within a specific mass range and may not facilitate the formation of very low mass cores.  Future observations using the ALMA global configuration are necessary to further refine the current core mass distribution findings.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, particularly concerning the conditions under which specific types of functions maintain their positive definiteness, have been extensively researched within the context of the Euclidean space.  When considering a sphere with a given dimension, the counterparts to these studies were initially limited until recently.  This paper extends the examination of positive definiteness for zonal functions and their expansions using Gegenbauer polynomials, specifically assessing the implications for the coefficients' behavior and the factors that determine the definitive nature of these coefficients in lower dimensional spaces.  Additionally, the Gegenbauer polynomial properties facilitate leveraging recurrence relations from positive definite functions to establish connections between the coefficients of the expansions of related functions that represent points relative to each other.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach of stress measurements using a novel rheological setup and molecular simulations, we have analyzed the impact of surface roughness on the flow of dense liquids. Our experimental stress measurements align closely with previous findings and provide a foundation for further analysis. We have identified and characterized three distinct friction regimes based on stress values: a low-stress regime with stress values below $10^{-4}$, where stress grows linearly with velocity slip and exhibits hysteresis; a moderate-stress regime where stress grows linearly with velocity slip but with a significantly higher friction coefficient; and a high-stress regime where stress increases super-linearly with velocity slip. Our analysis of simulation data reveals that these regimes correspond to different molecular responses to surface interactions and stress levels.

This report details our team's methodology for addressing the ISIC 2019 challenge, which focused on classifying skin lesions into categories such as nevus, melanoma, and other cancers. Our approach involved a comprehensive analysis of the provided dataset, critical discussions on data augmentation and augmentation techniques, and the development of a custom convolutional neural network. We also explored various methods to enhance the robustness and accuracy of our model. Ultimately, our team's solution secured third place in the challenge's public leaderboard.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, suspended between two fluids with different densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, is disrupted by fingering instability under certain conditions. The membrane's response to fluid density differences and centrifugal forces is modeled mathematically, and numerical methods are used to analyze nonlinear dynamics. Our findings reveal that the membrane initially forms drops at the outer radius and then undergoes shape transformations as centrifugal forces and tension interact. As rotation speed increases, point masses develop, interact, and eventually reconnect to form rings or toroidal structures. Notably, elastic properties play a key role in determining ring formation, whereas non-elastic models predict toroidal formation instead.

A significant discovery of ethynylbenine (C6H5CCH) in the direction of the Sgr A East source has been made through the observation of the 327.3644 MHz line corresponding to its 321->121 transition. Based on our density estimation, which is less than 4 x 10^4 cm-2, the detection of this molecule in the Galactic Center becomes feasible and the search for more complex organic compounds with higher dipole moments can be prioritized.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the history and development of high-performance computing to highlight and foster examples of beneficial advancements that represent successful translational computing.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed, combining a pressureless component, or dust-like dark matter, and a fluid component that can be described by the $\rho u^2$ parametrization. Although interactions within the dark sector are theoretically plausible, constraints from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and Cosmic Microwave Background observations require that this interaction be minimal or non-existent. A detailed perturbation analysis was carried out, demonstrating how the components of the unified dark fluid model exhibit distinct cosmological behaviors when interactions are minimal. These characteristics align with standard $\Lambda$CDM predictions, confirming that such a unified model can be an effective parametric representation of dark matter. Furthermore, we have derived the corresponding Boltzmann source terms and have verified that this model can be utilized in cosmic perturbation analyses. Furthermore, we have verified the consistency of cosmological parameters obtained from a background analysis with those from a perturbation analysis. However, we also showed that combining the components reverts to the unified dark fluid model.

Our research examines the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To address this, we analyzed J/ψ data from the B-factory experiments at the $	au$-energy level, focusing on precise measurements of J/ψ branching fractions into invisible matter at 1.6-GeV. By utilizing an effective Lagrangian, we established connections between these measurements and neutrinoless double beta decay, PMNS mixing angles, and light sterile neutrinos. We discovered that the J/ψ invisible decay width is directly related to heavy neutrino contributions to neutrinoless double beta decay and a specific combination of sterile and active neutrino mixing angles. We also established connections between the J/ψ invisible branching ratio and certain dark matter models, particularly those involving vector and scalar mediators coupled to electromagnetic and Weinberg operators. Analyzing J/ψ data from the B-factory allowed us to derive constraints on dark matter properties and theoretical coefficients, providing estimates for the dark matter density in the galaxy based on J/ψ production and decay in $	au$-collisions.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide, supported by an illustrative application. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through findings from a real-world dataset derived from a multivariate functional time series (VFTS) obtained from vector-valued functional magnetic resonance imaging (vfMRI) data, as well as an artificial VFTS generated using random fields. The results indicate that MFSSA outperforms the multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) method in terms of prediction accuracy for time series data. Additionally, the proposed methodology has the potential to yield more precise estimates of mean functions in addition to enhanced prediction accuracy.
